title: Stated time against actual time
question: Where the City or the State publishes a target or a time limit for a step, how does it compare with the time measured in the permit records?
finding: 9 published targets or limits could be set beside a measured figure. Planning's first plan review has a 30-day target and took a median 42 days in 2023 (60% over the deadline) and 28 in 2026 (12% over). A permit is now written to last 365 days, while permits taken out only to finish an earlier one found that earlier permit a median 4.4 years old. The table “permit types” prints a time for 145 permit pages, but almost all are advice on when to apply; only the State housing deadline matches a measured step.
how: Stated figures are read from the saved rule pages and reports (the number is taken from the text when the script runs). Measured figures are the medians already computed in the site’s “How the permit process works” page from City permit records. The ratio is measured days over stated days where both are in days.
limits: Most pairs do not share a clock, and the note on each row says how they differ: a target usually counts only the City's time on a complete application, while the records count everything from filing, including the applicant's own delays. A time limit is a ceiling, not a promise. The numeric targets for building permit review are published only in an interactive dashboard, which was not captured.

rows.measured: Median 135 days from a request being opened to closed, 2015 on
rows.note: Not the same clock: the measured figure runs from filing to closing of the record, which includes time after the hearing.

rows.step: Building permit application: time allowed before it expires
rows.stated: Application expires 730 days after filing unless extended
rows.measured: Full-review alterations issued in 2025 took a median 173 days; 45% of those issued in 2023 took over a year; 2,261 applications filed 2015 to 2023 ended unissued after a year or more
rows.note: The time limit is a ceiling, not a target. It applies to applications filed on or after June 21, 2026; the measured permits were under earlier limits.

rows.step: Issued building permit: life before it expires
rows.stated: Permit active 365 days, extended by each passed inspection
rows.measured: Permits taken out only to finish or renew an earlier permit: the earlier permit was a median 4.4 years old; 8,860 such permits since 2015
rows.note: Shows how long jobs outlive their permits, not a missed deadline: the 365-day rule took effect in 2026.

rows.step: New housing: decision on a complete building permit application (State law)

source.t: File an appeal of a permit or decision

rows.measured: New buildings issued in 2025 took a median 711 days from filing to issue
rows.note: Not the same clock: the State deadline runs from a complete application and excludes the applicant's time; the measured figure is filing to issue, all waiting included. The City's records cannot separate the two.

rows.step: Housing entitlement at Planning (Mayor's Executive Directive 17-02)
rows.stated: Approval hearing scheduled 6 to 22 months ahead, depending on the timeframe the directive sets for the project
rows.measured: Median 160 days from accepted application to approval, applications accepted since 2021 (all project types)
rows.note: The directive covers housing projects; the measured figure covers all Planning applications, most of them small. The lower end of the range (6 months, taken as 180 days) is used for the ratio.

rows.stated: Building Inspection reported 63% of applications handled within two business days (fiscal year 2023-2024)
rows.measured: Counter permits with plans worth $25,000 or more: 26% issued within a day for the fastest kind of applicant (licensed contractor), 6% for the slowest (permit consultant)
rows.note: Different measures: the department counts all counter applications and two business days; the measured figure counts larger counter jobs issued within one day.
